To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
training results in a significant reduction in whole-brain norepinephine and an increase in the ratio of 3-methoxyl-4-hydrophenylglycol to norepinephrines.

posttraining release in the brain of the catecholamine norepinephrin (NE) is correlated with later retention performance, but that the effects of amygdalectomy on NE levels are so pervasive as to make the results of amygdala stimulations difficult to interpret.
the effects of training in a memory task on the levels of brain catecholaminergic amines are widespread, and are correlated with the effects on memory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of training and amygdala stimulation upon memory.
the relationship between brain catecholaminergic activity and the acquisition, storage, and retrieval of information in memory.
the effects of training, amygdala damage, and amygdala stimulation, and their possible interactions, on brain catechols and memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results are consistent with the hypothesis that posttraining increases of NE levels in the neocortex, hippocampus, and other regions are correlated with enhanced memory.
the results of this study indicate that training produces a release of catecholamines in many brain regions which may be involved in memory storage.

the present results are consistent with the hypothesis that post-training release of brain NE is associated with the storage of new memory information, and that the effects of amygladal stimulation on memory may be mediated by changes in NE levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of training, amygdala stimulation, and amygdala damage are all very complex and cannot be understood in isolation from the other treatments.
post-training release of NE is widespread, but that the effects of amygladal stimulation on brain NE are not consistent with a general release.
training and amygdala stimulation have widespread effects on brain catecholes, which may reflect the involvement of these aminergic systems in memory storage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of training and amygdala stimulation cannot be interpreted without considering the baseline levels of brain amines in each animal.
brain catecholaminergic systems appear to play a role in the storage of memory, and that the effects of footshocks on memory are accompanied by changes in brain catecholaminoergic systems.
the effects of training, amygdala damage, and electrical stimulation of the brain on memory are not reflected in simple changes in brain levels of catecholamines.
